title: Numbers 14:26–38
context: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron the sentence. Every counted man twenty years and older who complained will die in the wilderness, except Caleb and Joshua. Their children, whom they feared would be captured or killed, will enter the land after forty years of wandering, one year for each day of scouting. The ten spies who spread the evil report die by plague, while Joshua and Caleb live.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron together, giving the formal sentence on the rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse the same way. This is shared ground.

verses.text: “How long shall I bear with this evil congregation that complain against me? I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel, which they complain against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “How long shall I bear with this evil congregation?” God’s patience has been tested repeatedly. Arminian readers stress that the judgment follows long forbearance and persistent resistance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see God’s long patience and the justice of the coming sentence. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Tell them, ‘As I live, says the LORD, surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.
verses.arminianNotes: God will do to them what they have said in his hearing. Their wish to die in the wilderness (verse 2) becomes their sentence. Judgment matches the sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same fitting justice. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness; and all who were counted of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have complained against me,
verses.arminianNotes: Everyone twenty years and older who was counted and complained will die in the wilderness. Hebrews 3:17 recalls those “whose bodies fell in the wilderness.” Arminian readers take this as a warning that people who began in God’s redemption can fall away through persistent unbelief, and they connect it with Hebrews 3:12, which warns against “an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear a real warning in Hebrews 3. They read the warnings as a means God uses to keep his people persevering, and they point to Hebrews 3:14, “For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end,” as showing that perseverance is the mark of true participation in Christ. On this reading, those who fall away show they never truly shared in Christ.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions agree that Hebrews uses the wilderness generation as a genuine warning to Christians, that unbelief is deadly, and that believers must persevere. Classical Arminians typically read the warning as describing a real possibility that true believers may fall away by persistent unbelief. Reformed interpreters typically read it as a means by which God preserves true believers, holding that those who finally fall away were never truly united to Christ. Both also note that the wilderness judgment itself concerned entering the land, so its relation to final salvation is debated within each tradition.

verses.text: surely you shall not come into the land concerning which I swore that I would make you dwell therein, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.
verses.arminianNotes: None will enter except Caleb and Joshua. God’s oath to the fathers stands, but this generation will not see it fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same contrast. God keeps his promise while judging those who refused it. This is shared ground.

verses.text: But I will bring in your little ones that you said should be captured or killed, and they shall know the land which you have rejected.
verses.arminianNotes: The little ones the people feared would be captured or killed will enter the land. God turns their unbelieving words back on them. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to his promise extended to the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s covenant faithfulness to the children. The promise is not cancelled by the parents’ unbelief. This is shared ground.

verses.text: But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness.” The sentence on the adults is stated plainly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse the same way. It is the source of the wording in Hebrews 3:17. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your prostitution, until your dead bodies are consumed in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The children will wander forty years and bear the consequences of their parents’ unfaithfulness, called “prostitution.” The innocent share in the effects of the guilty, though they are not condemned with them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that covenant unfaithfulness is pictured as spiritual adultery. The children suffer consequences but will receive the land. This is shared ground.

verses.text: After the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year, you will bear your iniquities, even forty years, and you will know my alienation.’
verses.arminianNotes: Forty days of scouting become forty years of bearing iniquity: a year for each day. Israel will “know my alienation,” meaning God’s opposition. The punishment is measured and deliberate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same correspondence of sin and sentence. This is shared ground.

verses.text: I, the LORD, have spoken. I will surely do this to all this evil congregation who are gathered together against me. In this wilderness they shall be consumed, and there they shall die.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD solemnly confirms the sentence on “this evil congregation” gathered against him. They will die in the wilderness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The certainty of God’s word applies to judgment as well as promise. This is shared ground.

verses.text: The men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation to murmur against him by bringing up an evil report against the land,
verses.arminianNotes: The spies who caused the congregation to murmur through their evil report are singled out. Leaders who mislead others bear particular responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same principle (compare James 3:1). This is shared ground.

verses.text: even those men who brought up an evil report of the land, died by the plague before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Those spies die by plague before the LORD. Their judgment is immediate, unlike the forty-year sentence on the rest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read this as a sign of the seriousness of leading others into unbelief. This is shared ground.

verses.text: But Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive of those men who went to spy out the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua and Caleb alone survive among the spies. God distinguishes the faithful from the unfaithful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see God preserving those who trusted him. This is shared ground.
